More than one

Content advisory: We discuss dissociation in this section of the guide.

You’ve probably heard of the term "more than one", most likely on the Am I Plural guide by The Dragonheart Collective! Plurality is being “more than one.”

What exactly is “more than one”? Essentially, it’s a state where there’s more than one consciousness within a body.

Maybe you have a computer terminal that helps you get through tough days. Maybe you have an introject of a character you fell in love with when you were twelve. Maybe you just hear a voice sometimes and it feels strange.

Simply put, a plural collective — or a system — is loosely defined as a group of consciousnesses having control of one body. This is oversimplifying it, of course — dissociation and plurality, as the community understands it, are spectra across two different axes. A lack of understanding by wider, neurotypical (and cishet) society probably hasn't helped.

Basic terms

Plurality, as defined by Pluralpedia, is the state of having multiple consciousnesses — or, colloquially, headmates — collectively sharing a single body. The opposite of plurality, where there’s only one consciousnesses in a body, is singlethood.

Plurality occurs when a person dissociates and loses some awareness of what’s happening around them. Most people dissociate some of the time, and it’s a fairly common thing! Dissociation occurs in various degrees of severity between folk, and can be worsened with exposure to trauma over long periods of time. It can manifest at times as either depersonalisation or derealisation.

Headmates are the colloquial term for these consciousnesses. They’re defined as a consciousness in a plural system, and can exist in clearly separated ways, or a more blurry and fluid way. Some may refer to headmates as alters, members, facets, or aspects.

A group of headmates can be referred to as a system, the collective of consciousnesses in a single physical plural body. Some systems contain sub-systems, a system within a system, defined as separate internal groups within a larger collective.

When a headmate is in control of the collective’s shared physical body, that is called fronting. When that control is swapped between headmates, that action is called switching. Some systems refer to switching a lot as “being switchy”, and it can be a sign of distress.

So what exactly does “more than one” mean?

There are many experiences about being "more than one" — plurality occurs on a spectrum, and a very diverse one!

The checklist below is adapted from The Dragonheart Collective's Am I Plural document which you can find here. Mark what feels familiar — tap or click once for a "maybe", and tap or click once for a "I experience this". You can also generate a shareable link that's useful to share with someone!

It's important to note that this checklist is here for you as a tool to understand yourself. It is not a diagnostic quiz. IT IS NOT A DIAGNOSTIC QUIZ.

We can't diagnose you with a dissociative disorder. Like the Dragonheart Collective, we are not psychologists. Experiencing something on this list doesn't mean that you have DID, OSDD, or DDNOS — all of which have their own diagnostic criteria. But you should note that these are experiences that are common to those who are plural.

Conversely, not experiencing something on this list doesn't mean that you are not plural, either. Saying no to some or all of the items on the list doesn't mean that you're not plural.

I said yes (or maybe) to some of these, but…

A lot of plurality is covert and difficult to notice.

Switching can feel like dramatic shifts in mood or personality — and could be explained away as that, mood swings.

It’s likely that your headmates have a more passive influence on front, perhaps, rather than jarringly being pushed to the front. Sudden switches aren’t common, in fact; most switches are likely passive.

Think about moments where you had to be confident for a presentation, perhaps. Maybe you felt really anxious in the run-up to the presentation, and you felt like you were about to have a panic attack — but when your name was called, you found a strange, confident voice within you that carried the presentation till its end, and the next thing you know you’re stunned to accept applause and have to awkwardly step off the stage. Later, when you step off the stage, you might realise you don’t exactly remember the emcee that introduced you, perhaps, or that the people in the room feel familiar, and that you have to try to remember their name.

That’s an example of passive influence — intrusions from parts of you that might carry you and help you in situations where you need to employ a skill you don’t usually have, or losing memory that you’d expect to be there.

It’s also likely that you’ll forget what you forgot. While reviewing the checklist, we (the 󱤟 Pleiadesfolk) realised that we couldn’t identify fully with some of these signs, even when we understood ourselves as a system.

For instance, we didn’t feel like we’ve “lost time”, but describe time as something that either stretches or compresses depending on whose perspective it is; we can look at a clock and realise that it’s 10 p.m. before realising that we didn’t have any dinner. Still, both of these are “lost time”.

Episodic memory for us can be spotty — we might struggle with talking about what we did on a day to our partner, only for a fronter to appear and say “oh, I put in 200 more words on our story!” when prompted. More frequently, we might struggle to talk about what happened at work, perhaps.

Memory weirdness

It’s likely that memory gaps, for many of us, aren’t going to be Big or Obvious. Memory segmentation can happen in many ways. Emotion can be segmented away, and so would other qualities of a memory — narratives or context.

You might just not feel anything at all about that memory gap — and you’re usually not going to notice. Tumblr user semiplural notes:

I think of our memory as being like train tracks. Sometimes the tracks run together, sometimes they don't. You're usually not going to notice a missing track unless you look out the window of your own train, and you're too busy driving it to do that.

You're more likely to notice when entering or exiting the train (switching).

Recovering some of your memories will take some work, which we explore here.

I’m probably faking all of this!

Consider that you just probably opened this handbook. Faking requires that you intentionally know and understand how to fake something. You can’t fake plurality by accident.

The top feeling that plural systems get is that they’re “faking this for attention.” Your brain essentially doesn’t want you to know that all this is happening; in particular, your brain may be protecting you against traumatic memories that remain unresolved, and your brain might want to preserve some semblance of identity in order for you to function. So at times, this might feel like: “Hey! I don’t remember how to do this, but now I do?”

Plurality in general presents itself in a covert fashion.

From Patricia Taxxon:

You don’t usually notice it if you have it. It doesn’t necessarily involve blacking out at random times or waking up in weird places. Instead of blacking out, you’re more likely to slowly forget and seamlessly transition into a new personality without a break in “consciousness” as a whole.

(…) You might hear your voice change its tone in an imperceptible way, and need to be reminded of a couple of things you were talking about, before seamlessly continuing function.

(…) A big universal symptom of plurality is denial.

To fight the feeling that you're faking all of this, you'll have to make a conscious effort to unmask and perform. You type differently, speak differently, adopt a mannerism comfortable to you even if it feels different.

As Patricia Taxxon says: “This is just vital mental health work. I don’t know how any system is supposed to disambiguate and forge lines of communication without a little theatre.”

Does adopting this framework actually work?

Theatre. That word evokes emotions of faking it all, pretense. Everything’s just an “act”, maybe. It’s all a fiction! They’re just voices, and they’re just all in your head!

Counterpoint: of course it’s all in your head, that’s where your headmates live!

So why adopt this framework? Adopting this framework means that you give other parts of you a chance to interact with the world or speak aloud.

The other yous — your headmates — might not seem as distinct. Most of us overlap a bit (more on that later). But to air their desires — and for them to air their desires to you — allows you to be more aware of what they’re thinking or feeling.

Is it all real? Is it all in our head? Does it matter?

From the Vicki(s):

What matters is what “works". Does it work if you treat those voices as other parts, or alters? Does it work if you listen to what they have to say, treat them respectfully as "valid" points of view? Does it work to let those voices out to tell their own story in their own words, to feel their feelings?

(…) I would go through phases of feeling like I was making it all up, that I was overdramatizing, that what I was doing was silly, that I was just being influenced by my friends, etc etc etc.

(And in case you’re going “this is all newfangled bullshit”, this was written in 1998. Plurals have always existed, and they’ve always felt like they’re faking it.)

Notably, not adopting this framework might mean that you heavily suppress some of the more difficult-to-deal-with emotions — self-hatred, disgust, dysphoria, self-destructive tendencies — and that might mean that their emotions would leak through, slowly but surely, into your own psyche.

Parts that possess these difficult-to-deal-with emotions will need time to process them, carefully and slowly, and this framework will help with that.
